title: Introducing Casco Cloud Security
summary: Introducing Casco Cloud Security: prioritize cloud risk, follow resource and IAM relationships, and investigate suspicious activity. Try it with the interactive Koalemos challenge.
body_markdown:
# Introducing Casco Cloud Security


Written by


[Casco Team](https://casco.com/)


on


Mon Nov 23 2026


**If every alert is a priority, then nothing gets fixed. That’s the problem we’re solving.**


Cloud security tools can leave teams buried in alerts. Every vulnerable package, exposed resource, and broad permission gets its own place in the queue. When everything looks urgent, choosing what to fix becomes another job, and the backlog keeps growing.


Today we’re launching[Casco Cloud Security](https://casco.com/features/cloud-security) to help break that cycle. It connects cloud resources, vulnerabilities, network configuration, and IAM relationships so your team can investigate what matters, see the evidence, and decide what to fix. Real-time threat detection brings suspicious activity from the logs you enable into the same investigation.


## Watch the two-minute walkthrough


[Watch on YouTube](https://youtu.be/51ghWbI9dhQ) .


Koalemos is a sample invoicing app for a fictional startup. Explore its website and cloud setup to see what Casco Cloud Security finds.


Explore the Koalemos sample app


[Open full screen ↗](https://casco.com/demos/koalemos/index.html)


## Start with the risk, then check the evidence


An EC2 instance with a vulnerable package is one finding. Add public exposure and broad IAM permissions, and there is more to investigate. The useful question is what that combination could let an attacker do.


Open a finding to review the signals behind it. Inspect the source observation, analysis, and provider recommendation, and check whether runtime validation has been performed. A vulnerable package report alone does not establish reachability or demonstrated impact. Your team should be able to tell what is supported by evidence and what still needs testing.


## Ask what an attacker could reach next


An exposed workload is the start of an investigation. Could it connect to another resource? Which identity does it use? What permissions could extend its reach?


Casco’s security graph puts network and IAM relationships in view, with findings and threats alongside the resources they affect. **Find path** lets you select two resources and examine the connections between them. An EC2 → IAM → S3 path gives the team a concrete place to investigate potential lateral movement. Effective access still depends on the applicable policies and conditions.


That context helps explain why a finding deserves attention: the exposure, vulnerability, and permissions can be considered together, along with what else may be reachable.


Where source context is available, Casco also links deployed resources to their repository and package or module, with match confidence, giving engineers a place to look in the code.


## Bring suspicious activity into the investigation


Potential paths tell you where to look. Activity logs add another question: what is happening now? Casco detects suspicious activity in real time using the log sources you enable, then keeps the actor, affected resources, timeline, and supporting evidence together.


An access key used from an unexpected geography needs an explanation. Open the investigation to review the events behind the alert and track its assessment, status, and owner as the investigation progresses. That gives the next person a clear place to pick up the work.


## Connect the scope you choose


Casco Cloud Security supports AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Connect the accounts and resources you choose with read-only access, and enable the logs needed for threat monitoring. Coverage depends on the provider, services, and permissions connected. Your team controls any production response.


[Book a demo](https://casco.com/book) to see which cloud risks deserve your team’s attention.


**Get your head in the cloud.**
